**Observation Log:**

[TEMPORAL] Session Date: 2023/07/11 (Tue) 23:27  
[USER] User asked if Monte Carlo integration can be used to integrate f(x).  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant confirmed that Monte Carlo integration can be used to approximate the definite or indefinite integral of a function using random sampling.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The method involves generating random points within the region of integration and using the function to evaluate the points.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The average value of the function at these points is used as an estimate of the definite integral or area under the curve of the function.  
[USER] User requested an example in C++.  
[ASSISTANT_CREATED] Assistant provided a C++ code example for Monte Carlo integration to approximate the definite integral of f(x) = x^2 from 0 to 1 using 10,000 random points.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The function `monte_carlo_integration` takes three arguments: the lower bound of integration, upper bound of integration, and number of random points.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The code estimates the definite integral and notes that accuracy depends on the number of random points used.  
[USER] User asked how to integrate f(x) = e^(-x^2/2).  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant explained that Monte Carlo integration can be used similarly by generating random points and evaluating the function at those points.  
[ASSISTANT_CREATED] Assistant provided a C++ code example for Monte Carlo integration of f(x) = e^(-x^2/2) from -3 to 3 using 10,000 random points.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The assistant noted that this is an approximation method and the error decreases with more samples.  
[USER] User inquired about estimating the uncertainty of the integral computed using Monte Carlo.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant explained that the uncertainty can be estimated using the standard deviation of the function values at the randomly generated points.  
[ASSISTANT_CREATED] Assistant provided a C++ code snippet that calculates the standard deviation along with the integral estimate.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The variance is calculated as (total_sq/n - (total/n)^2) * (b - a)^2, and the standard deviation is the square root of the variance.  
[USER] User asked how to write the same code in Python.  
[ASSISTANT_CREATED] Assistant provided a Python code example for Monte Carlo integration with uncertainty estimation for f(x) = e^(-x^2/2).  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The Python code approximates the definite integral from -3 to 3 using 10,000 random points and includes the calculation of standard deviation.
